boards.title: Only Happens Here: 10 Traditions That Make No Sense Anywhere Else
boards.description: Ten documented Kenyon rituals, songs, superstitions and ceremonies that mark students’ passage from arrival through Commencement.

cards.title: Sing Four Kenyon Songs Before Classes Begin
cards.subtitle: New students take the Rosse Hall steps during Orientation
cards.notes: Bring the provided song sheet, face the crowd from the Rosse Hall steps and listen for returning students joining “Kokosing Farewell.”
cards.short_summary: Kenyon introduces each incoming class through a public performance of four College songs.
cards.evidence_claim: Kenyon documents new students gathering on the Rosse Hall steps with song sheets while Professor Benjamin “Doc” Locke conducts and returning students cheer them on.
cards.access_notes: The Sing is associated with new-student Orientation; returning students traditionally watch and sing from the audience.

cards.title: Return to the Steps for a Final Sing
cards.subtitle: Seniors reprise Kenyon songs during Commencement Weekend
cards.notes: Watch for the graduating class on Rosse Hall’s steps the Friday before Commencement, returning to songs learned at the start of college.
cards.short_summary: The first and last sings bookend a Kenyon student’s time on the Hill.
cards.evidence_claim: Kenyon reports that the annual Senior Sing tradition occurred on the Rosse Hall steps during 2026 Commencement Weekend, following Baccalaureate.
cards.access_notes: Senior Sing is a graduating-class Commencement Weekend activity; spectators should follow the College’s published ceremony arrangements.

cards.title: Add One Name to a Book Begun in 1841
cards.subtitle: New students sign Kenyon’s leather-bound Matriculation Book
cards.notes: After taking the oath, follow the announced signing instructions and add your name carefully beside generations of earlier Kenyon students.
cards.short_summary: A handwritten signature physically links each new student to Kenyon classes stretching back to the nineteenth century.
cards.evidence_claim: Kenyon states that students who take the Matriculation Oath are invited to sign the Matriculation Book, whose signatures date to 1841 and include Rutherford B. Hayes.
cards.access_notes: Signing is for eligible new students after the oath; Kenyon announces the location and any make-up period for each Founders’ Day.

cards.title: Become a Kenyon Student by Saying the Oath
cards.subtitle: First-year and transfer students make a shared Founders’ Day pledge
cards.notes: Join the spoken pledge during Founders’ Day, then proceed to the Matriculation Book when College staff invite your cohort to sign.
cards.short_summary: Formal membership begins with a communal promise rather than merely a first day of class.
cards.evidence_claim: Kenyon says its Matriculation Oath was instituted in 1841 and is taken by all first-year and transfer students during the Founders’ Day program.
cards.access_notes: Participation is for first-year and transfer students as part of the formal Founders’ Day program.

cards.title: Plant the Incoming Class’s Tree
cards.subtitle: Each new class leaves a living gift on Kenyon’s grounds
cards.notes: Follow the post-ceremony gathering to see the class tree planted and its name revealed; remain outside the marked work area.
cards.short_summary: The incoming class marks its arrival with a tree intended to represent continuity and environmental stewardship.
cards.evidence_claim: Kenyon states that the incoming class plants a tree after the Founders’ Day ceremony to symbolize growth, continuity and preservation of the campus environment.
cards.access_notes: The planting follows Founders’ Day; the precise campus site and participation arrangements may vary by class year.

cards.title: Read the Names That Joined Kenyon’s Story
cards.subtitle: Founders’ Day pauses to remember community members who died
cards.notes: Listen quietly as a faculty member reads the annual memorial, which closes by calling the Kenyon community toward justice and peace.
cards.short_summary: Kenyon’s fall convocation remembers both its founders and recently deceased members of the College community.
cards.evidence_claim: Kenyon documents an annual Founders’ Memorial in which a faculty member reads names of prominent alumni and members of the faculty, staff, administration and student body who died in the preceding year.
cards.access_notes: The memorial is part of the formal Founders’ Day ceremony; observe the respectful character of the reading.

cards.title: Step Around the Seal, Just in Case
cards.subtitle: A graduation superstition shapes foot traffic inside Peirce Hall
cards.notes: Notice how people route around the inlaid seal at Peirce’s entrance; the four-year consequence is campus legend, not an established fact.
cards.short_summary: A shiny floor emblem has become the center of Kenyon’s playful graduation superstition.
cards.evidence_claim: A Kenyon student-life article says students avoid stepping on the Peirce Hall seal because legend claims doing so prevents graduation within four years.
cards.source_title: Caution! This List Will Make You Nostalgic
cards.access_notes: Peirce Hall is a working campus dining facility; view the seal without obstructing entrances or meal-service traffic.

cards.title: Hear the Academic Week End in Bells
cards.subtitle: Kenyon Pealers fill campus with changing tunes on Friday afternoons
cards.notes: Pause outdoors near the end of the academic week and listen for a program that may range from hymns and carols to film themes.
cards.short_summary: A weekly peal turns the Church of the Holy Spirit’s bells into Kenyon’s Friday soundtrack.
cards.evidence_claim: A Kenyon student-life article documents the Kenyon Pealers playing the Church of the Holy Spirit bells every Friday afternoon, with music audible across campus.
cards.source_title: Caution! This List Will Make You Nostalgic
cards.access_notes: Listen from public campus grounds; bell access and performance participation are restricted to authorized Pealers.

cards.title: Choose a Side Before Passing the Gates
cards.subtitle: Students share an unexplained Middle Path walking custom
cards.notes: Approach the stone pillars normally and stay with your companion’s chosen side; the cited account documents the custom, not its meaning.
cards.short_summary: Even an ordinary walk through two stone pillars comes with an unwritten Kenyon rule.
cards.evidence_claim: The Kenyon Collegian describes walking on the same side as others through the campus feature called the “Gates of Hell” as a commonplace Kenyon tradition.
cards.source_title: From the Archives: Traditions for Greeting New Presidents
cards.access_notes: This is a walking custom on Middle Path, not an invitation to climb the pillars, enter restricted areas or visit after campus access closes.

cards.title: Graduate Between Two Columns of Faculty
cards.subtitle: Seniors process south along Middle Path toward Commencement
cards.notes: Watch from outside the procession route as seniors travel south between faculty columns, mirroring the ceremonial start of college.
cards.short_summary: Kenyon frames a student’s college career with formal passages along its central gravel path.
cards.evidence_claim: Kenyon’s alumni archive states that since 1978 seniors have marched south on Middle Path through two columns of faculty members on their way to Commencement exercises.
cards.source_title: A Path for All Seasons (Even February?)
cards.access_notes: The academic procession is a formal Commencement activity; spectators should use designated viewing areas and keep Middle Path clear.
